title: How does String concatenation work internally (compiler using StringBuilder, constant folding for compile-time constants, and why to use StringBuilder in loops)?
shortTitle: How does String concatenation work internally?

s1_definition.profdef: Java String concatenation with the plus operator is compiled into efficient code rather than naive string copying. For compile-time constant operands, the compiler folds them into a single literal at compile time, so there is no runtime work. For runtime operands, older compilers translated a plus b into a `StringBuilder` append chain, and since Java 9 the compiler uses the `invokedynamic`-based `StringConcatFactory` which the JVM optimizes further. The problem arises with concatenation inside loops: each loop iteration creates a fresh builder and a new immutable String, producing quadratic time and heavy garbage, which is why you should use an explicit `StringBuilder` declared once outside the loop and append inside it.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, building a statement string with plus in a loop is like a clerk who, for every new transaction line, recopies the entire statement onto a fresh sheet of paper and throws the old sheet away. For a thousand transactions that is a thousand full recopies, wasting enormous paper and time. The smart clerk instead uses one long scroll, a StringBuilder, and simply writes each new line at the bottom without recopying anything. The compiler is clever enough to handle a single plus efficiently, and it even pre-computes concatenations that are entirely fixed text, but it cannot rescue a loop that keeps rebuilding the whole string, so the clerk must choose the scroll.
s1_definition.oneliner: Constant concatenations fold at compile time, a single plus is optimized by the compiler, but concatenation in a loop is quadratic, so use one StringBuilder outside the loop.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Java String concatenation with the plus operator is compiled into efficient code rather than naive string copying. For compile-time constant operands, the compiler folds them into a single literal at compile time, so there is no runtime work. For runtime operands, older compilers translated a plus b into a `StringBuilder` append chain, and since Java 9 the compiler uses the `invokedynamic`-based `StringConcatFactory` which the JVM optimizes further. The problem arises with concatenation inside loops: each loop iteration creates a fresh builder and a new immutable String, producing quadratic time and heavy garbage, which is why you should use an explicit `StringBuilder` declared once outside the loop and append inside it.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, building a statement string with plus in a loop is like a clerk who, for every new transaction line, recopies the entire statement onto a fresh sheet of paper and throws the old sheet away. For a thousand transactions that is a thousand full recopies, wasting enormous paper and time. The smart clerk instead uses one long scroll, a StringBuilder, and simply writes each new line at the bottom without recopying anything. The compiler is clever enough to handle a single plus efficiently, and it even pre-computes concatenations that are entirely fixed text, but it cannot rescue a loop that keeps rebuilding the whole string, so the clerk must choose the scroll.

**One line to remember:** Constant concatenations fold at compile time, a single plus is optimized by the compiler, but concatenation in a loop is quadratic, so use one StringBuilder outside the loop.

sections.s2_technical:
For compile-time constants, the compiler performs constant folding. If you write the literal Account colon plus the literal SAV2001, both constants, the compiler computes the final string at compile time and stores it as a single literal in the constant pool. There is zero runtime concatenation, and the result is even pooled.

For runtime operands, a single concatenation expression like a plus b plus c, where some parts are variables, is compiled efficiently. Before Java 9, javac generated a `StringBuilder`, appended each part, and called toString. From Java 9 onward, javac emits an `invokedynamic` instruction bound to `StringConcatFactory`, which lets the JVM choose and optimize the concatenation strategy at runtime, often avoiding intermediate allocations. Either way, a single concatenation statement is handled well and you do not need to hand-optimize it.

The real problem is concatenation inside a loop. Because String is immutable, each plus in each iteration cannot modify the existing string; it must build a new String containing everything so far plus the new piece. So in a loop that appends to a result string, iteration one copies one piece, iteration two copies two pieces, iteration three copies three pieces, and so on. The total work grows with the square of the number of iterations, which is quadratic time, and it allocates a new String and often a new builder each time, flooding the garbage collector. For a statement with thousands of lines, this is a serious performance problem.

The fix is to declare a single `StringBuilder` once before the loop and call append inside the loop. StringBuilder maintains a growable char buffer, so each append is amortized constant time and there is one final toString. This turns quadratic work into linear work with far less garbage. A senior nuance is that the compiler's per-statement optimization does not span loop iterations, which is why you still must use an explicit builder for loops; the compiler cannot prove it is safe to reuse a builder across your loop. Another nuance is to size the builder with an initial capacity when you can estimate the final length, avoiding internal array resizes, which matters when generating large banking statements or reports.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank generates a monthly statement by concatenating many transaction lines. The first version used plus in a loop and became painfully slow for active accounts with thousands of transactions. This is exactly the quadratic concatenation problem.

Problem 2 — The fixed version uses a single StringBuilder with a sensible initial capacity, appending each line, producing the same statement far faster with less garbage. This is exactly the StringBuilder-in-loop fix.

Problem 3 — The header line uses only constant text, which the compiler folds at compile time, showing constant folding. This is exactly compile-time constant handling.

The code has a `StatementGenerator` with both a slow and a fast method, and a `ConcatDemo` main class that times both.
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/report/ConcatDemo.java

# Run (observe slow method is dramatically slower than fast method)
java -cp out com.bank.report.ConcatDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an account SAV2001 and 20000 statement lines, generated by both the slow and fast methods.

Step 1: The HEADER constant is defined by concatenating three literals. The compiler folds these into a single literal at compile time, so at runtime HEADER is just one pooled string with no concatenation work.

Step 2: The slow method starts with a result string and, in each of 20000 iterations, uses plus to build a new string equal to everything so far plus the new line. Because String is immutable, each iteration copies the entire accumulated text.

Step 3: As the loop progresses, each iteration copies more and more characters, so total work grows with the square of the line count, and thousands of intermediate String and builder objects are created and discarded, stressing the garbage collector.

Step 4: The fast method creates one StringBuilder with a pre-sized capacity and appends each line into its internal buffer without recopying the accumulated text. Each append is amortized constant time.

Step 5: After the loop, a single toString produces the final statement. The total work is linear in the number of lines, with far less garbage.

Step 6: Both methods produce identical content, confirmed by equals, but the fast method is dramatically quicker, demonstrating why StringBuilder is required for loops while the compiler already handles single concatenations and constants.

```text
WARNING: slow (+ in loop) ms = 1680, length=620019
INFO: fast (StringBuilder) ms = 3, length=620019
INFO: same content: true
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  HEADER = "National"+" Bank"+" of India"  (all constants)
    │ compiler constant-folds → ONE literal "National Bank of India"
    ▼ no runtime concat

  ─── slow: + in loop (quadratic) ───
  iter0: copy [0..n0]      ┐
  iter1: copy [0..n0+n1]   ├─ each iter recopies ALL prior chars
  ...                      ┘   → O(n^2) time, O(n) garbage objects
  result grows by full recopy each time

  ─── fast: one StringBuilder (linear) ───
  sb (growable buffer) ← append, append, append ... (no recopy)
    │ toString() once at end
    ▼ O(n) time, minimal garbage
```

  │ Net Banking│─────────→ │ StatementService │───────→ │ PDF / S3     │
  └────────────┘           │ StringBuilder    │         └──────────────┘

sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Concatenation Strategy Decision ═══

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Scenario                    Best approach       │
  │ ─────────────────────────────────────────────│
  │ all constants ("A"+"B")     compiler folds → literal │
  │ single statement a+b+c      leave to compiler (StringConcatFactory) │
  │ concatenation in a LOOP     explicit StringBuilder  │
  │ concurrent building          StringBuffer (synced)   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  StringBuilder internals:
    - char[]/byte[] value (growable)
    - count (used length)
    - append() writes in place, resizes (×2) when full
    - pre-size with new StringBuilder(estimatedLength) to avoid resizes
  Complexity: + in loop → O(n^2) ; StringBuilder loop → O(n)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Java String concatenation with the plus operator is compiled into efficient code, not naive copying, and understanding the three cases is the key. For compile-time constants, the compiler does constant folding: if I concatenate literals, it computes the final string at compile time and stores it as a single pooled literal, so there is no runtime work at all. For a single runtime concatenation statement, like a plus b plus c where some parts are variables, the compiler handles it efficiently; before Java 9 it generated a StringBuilder append chain, and from Java 9 onward it emits an invokedynamic instruction bound to the StringConcatFactory, which lets the JVM optimize the strategy at runtime. So I do not need to hand-optimize a single concatenation.

The real problem is concatenation inside a loop. Because String is immutable, each plus in each iteration cannot modify the existing string; it must build a new String containing everything accumulated so far plus the new piece. So iteration by iteration it copies more and more characters, and the total work grows with the square of the number of iterations, which is quadratic, while also allocating a new String each time and flooding the garbage collector. For a statement with thousands of transaction lines, this is a serious performance problem, and I measured one version taking well over a second for twenty thousand lines.

The fix is to declare a single StringBuilder once before the loop and append inside it. StringBuilder keeps a growable buffer, so each append is amortized constant time, there is one final toString, and the quadratic cost collapses to linear with far less garbage; the same twenty thousand lines then took a few milliseconds. The reason the compiler cannot do this for me is that its per-statement optimization does not span loop iterations, so it cannot prove it is safe to reuse a builder across my loop.

In our statement generation service this is exactly how I build large statements: a single StringBuilder, pre-sized with an estimated capacity to avoid internal array resizes, appending each transaction line. And when the building is concurrent, I reach for StringBuffer instead, which is the thread-safe synchronized sibling. The summary I give is: constants fold at compile time, single concatenations are optimized by the compiler, but loops demand an explicit StringBuilder.

---

keyPoints: Compiler optimizes constant concatenation at compile time
Variable concatenation: Java 9+ uses invokedynamic + StringConcatFactory
In loops, each + may create objects — use StringBuilder explicitly
String.join() or Collectors.joining() for collection concatenation
